MESOPOTAMIA · A MODERN AUDIBLE REALIZATION

Sammû · listening practice

2 retuning moves · initial string 1: 440 Hz · companion strings: octave · sound: sine

An audible fourths-and-fifths realization, not a recovered ancient performance. Six designated pairs are set to frequency ratios 4/3 or 3/2. Reference pitch, numerical precision, sound colour and the companion-string octave/unison choice are modern settings. The tablets do not record frequencies in hertz or these fractions.

This file includes its fonts, diagram, audio and numerical record. Open it offline, or use your browser’s Print command to save a PDF. External source links need a connection.

Read the procedure and its preservation

These are our summaries of three neighboring cases in the published translation. A supplied scribal omission and a restoration across damaged text are different kinds of editorial intervention.

išartum → kitmum

Begin in išartum. Test qablītum, strings 5 + 2. Loosen the following string and the back string: 2 + 9. The resulting tuning is kitmum.

The word describing the pair as unclear is supplied by the editor as an omission, marked ⟨ ⟩ in the edition. The case is not an entirely untouched ancient sentence.

Loosening section, lines 13–16; Mirelman 2013, pp. 49–52.

kitmum → embūbum

Begin in kitmum. Test išartum, strings 2 + 6. Loosen the fourth string from behind: 6. The reconstructed result is embūbum.

The result clause is restored across a break, marked [ ] in the edition. The diagnostic pair and action are preserved in the published translation.

Loosening section, lines 17–20; Mirelman 2013, pp. 51–52.

embūbum → pītum

The reconstructed case tests kitmum, strings 6 + 3, and loosens string 3. Its destination is pītum.

Almost all of this case is restored in [ ]; the final tuning name survives. Its place in the pattern is an editorial reconstruction, not an equally preserved instruction.

Loosening section, lines 21–24; Mirelman 2013, p. 52.

Akkadian word notes

Normalized romanization, with selected meanings in this context. The notes distinguish a preserved action word from a restored interpretation.

sammû
a stringed instrument

Its precise identification as harp or lyre is unsettled. The diagram here describes string relationships, not its archaeological shape.

zakû
clear / clean / pure

A source term for a pair of strings. Its musical meaning is interpreted; it is not a recorded numerical frequency ratio.

lā zakû
not clear

The diagnostic pair distinguishes one named tuning from another. The spelling here is normalized Akkadian romanization.

išartum
straight / normal

Both the name of strings 2 + 6 and the name of a tuning. Pair names and tuning names do different jobs.

kitmum
closed

A tuning name and a pair name: strings 6 + 3. The same pair can be clear in one tuning and unclear in another.

qablītum
middle

Names strings 5 + 2. In išartum tuning this is the diagnostic unclear pair; after loosening string 2 it is clear.

nê'um
to loosen

Intact and partly preserved forms occur in the loosening chapter. They support the physical direction assigned to that action. See Rahn (2022), paragraph 45.

nasāḫum
to remove / subtract; ‘tighten’ here

Editors restore the verb in the tightening instructions. A partly preserved concluding rubric supports this contextual interpretation. It does not mean ‘tighten’ in every Akkadian setting. See Rahn (2022), paragraph 45.

šumma
if

Introduces a condition. In a procedural case, distinguish that condition from the instructed action and its result. Lexical support: Høyrup (2017), Appendix B; the tuning text’s conditional format is discussed by Mirelman (2013), pp. 49–50.

How to read this model

Six pairs of strings are assigned exact 4/3 or 3/2 frequency ratios. The remaining diagnostic pair is left unclear. Each operation changes only the prescribed string (and its companion for strings 1 or 2), making that diagnostic pair clear. The next diagnostic pair then becomes unclear.

Seven moves in one direction return the tuning name but shift every string by 2048/2187 when loosening, or 2187/2048 when tightening. These fractions are consequences of this model, not ratios written on a tablet. No ancient reference pitch, recorded performance, instrument shape, or exact ancient sound colour is claimed.

The two tuning manuscripts from Ur are fragmentary. Combining them with later string-pair evidence is a scholarly reconstruction. In Mirelman’s edition, supplied scribal omissions use ⟨ ⟩ and text restored across a break uses [ ]. For example, the first loosening case has an editorially supplied description of the diagnostic pair; the third is mostly restored.

Sources and provenance

  1. Sam Mirelman · Tuning Procedures in Ancient Iraq (2013)

    Analytical Approaches to World Music 2(2), 43–56. String names: p. 46; two manuscripts and uncertain instrument: pp. 47–48; preserved/restored clauses: pp. 49–52; seven tunings: fig. 5, p. 52; tightening: pp. 53–54.

  2. Jay Rahn · Was Mesopotamian Tuning Diatonic? A Parsimonious Answer (2022)

    Music Theory Online 28.1. DOI 10.30535/mto.28.1.7. Paragraphs 9–16 distinguish physical strings from later pitch concepts and explain the reversible seven-name network; later sections examine assumptions behind an audible reconstruction.

  3. Sam Mirelman & Theo J. H. Krispijn · The Old Babylonian tuning text UET VI/3 899 (2009)

    Iraq 71, 43–52. Edition of the second manuscript. Read with UET VII 74; the two witnesses are separate tablets, not joining fragments of one tablet.

  4. CDLI P347039 · UET VII 74

    Catalogue record for one tuning manuscript from Ur, Old Babylonian period. The British Museum witness discussed by Mirelman is a cast; do not infer the original tablet’s present location from the catalogue’s collection field.

  5. CDLI P254475 · CBS 10996

    Later witness for named string pairs. The catalogue checked on 22 October 2026 assigns Middle Babylonian, approximately 1400–1100 BCE; Mirelman (2013) used an older Neo-Babylonian dating. Combining witnesses is a scholarly reconstruction across time.

  6. Jens Høyrup · Algebra in Cuneiform, Appendix B (2017)

    Key to Vocabulary and Standard Translations: šumma, ‘if’. This is lexical support from a study of mathematical texts, not another witness to the musical procedure. The action verbs are discussed by Rahn (2022), paragraph 45.
